Part A - Creating Matrices
```{r}
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1
```

```{r}
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
```

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores
```
Question #1:

Compare m1 and m2 above. Both were built from 1:9 with nrow = 3, ncol = 3, but they look different.
Explain exactly what byrow = TRUE changes about how R fills a matrix.
    
    R fills a matrix column by column by default (down the first column, then down the second, and so on). Instead, R fills the matrix row by row (across the first row, then across the second) when byrow = TRUE is added.
    
Question #2

If you tried matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3) (only 8 numbers for 9 slots), what do you think would happen?
Test it and explain the result, including any warning message.
    
    R will still fill all 9 slots by reusing or recycling the numbers from the beginning even if you only enter 8 numbers into a 3 x 3 matrix, which requires 9 values. The first value (1) will be entered into the ninth slot, and a warning message indicating that the data length is neither a multiple nor a sub-multiple of the row length will be displayed.

Part B — Subsetting Matrices
```{r}
scores[1, 2]
scores[1, ]
scores[, "Ben"]
```

```{r}
scores[scores >= 90]
```
Question #3

scores[1, ] and scores[, "Ben"] both return a result, but one represents a row and the other a column.
Run class() on each result. What data structure does R “downgrade” a single row/column of a matrix to, and why do you think R does this automatically?
    
    R converts a single row or column from a matrix to a "numeric" standard 1D vector. Because a single row or column no longer needs a 2D grid structure, R does this automatically to save memory and streamline operations.
    
Question #4

In the matrix-logical chunk, the row/column names disappeared from your result. * Why does subsetting with a logical condition (scores >= 90) lose the 2D shape and names thatscores[1, ] kept?
    
    Logical subsetting extracts only the numbers that match TRUE by evaluating each value in the matrix separately against the condition (such as >= 90). R flattens the result into a straightforward 1D vector, removing the row/column labels and matrix dimensions because the matching values can originate from anywhere in the grid.
    
Part C — Matrix Properties and Operations
```{r}
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)

scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t
dim(scores_t)
```

```{r}
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)

a + b
a * b
```

```{r}
a %*% b
```
Question #5

a * b and a %*% b both “multiply” the same two matrices but give different results.
Explain the difference between element-wise multiplication and matrix multiplication in your own words.
    
    Simply multiplying matching positions together (top-left times top-left, bottom-right times bottom-right) is element-wise multiplication (a * b). By taking the dot product of the rows from the first matrix and the columns from the second, matrix multiplication (a %*% b) adheres to the rules of linear algebra.
    
Question #6

t(scores) swaps rows and columns. Look at dim(scores) versus dim(scores_t).
Why must the row/column names also swap positions when you transpose a matrix?
    
    When a matrix is transposed, the entire grid is flipped across its diagonal, transforming rows into columns and columns into rows. In order to maintain accurate labeling of the data, row values' labels must switch places since they are now column values.
    
Part D — cbind() and rbind()
```{r}
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2
```

```{r}
scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```
Question #7 * What would happen if you tried cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) — giving 3 values for a matrix that only has 2 rows? * Test it, read the warning/error, and explain why cbind() and rbind()) require matching dimensions.
    
    Because scores has only two rows while the new vector has three values, running cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) causes an error. In order to ensure that every row or column contains complete data without any misaligned or missing slots, both cbind() and rbind() require matching dimensions along the boundary being combined.
    
Question #8

In what situation would you use rbind() instead of cbind() when updating a dataset over time?
Give a concrete example (e.g., daily sales, weekly attendance) and explain your reasoning.
    
    When adding new observations over time while maintaining the same set of variables, you would use rbind() rather than cbind(). For instance, every new day's sales figures are added as a new row at the bottom of the dataset in a daily sales tracker where columns represent product categories.
    
Part E — Arrays: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr

arr[1, 2, 2]
arr[, , 1]
dim(arr)
```
Question #9

A matrix needs 2 indices (scores[row, col]) but an array needs 3 (arr[row, col, layer]).
Using dim(arr), explain in your own words what each of the three numbers represents.
    
    The result of dim(arr) is c(2, 3, 2). The number of rows in each matrix is represented by the first number (2), the number of columns by the second number (3), and the number of 2D slices (layers) stacked in the 3D array by the third number (2).
    
Question #10

Give a real-world example of data that would naturally fit a 3D array structure (hint: think of something that has rows, columns, AND a third repeating dimension like time, subjects, or categories).

Explain why a single 2D matrix would not be enough.
    
    Monthly weather monitoring in several cities is a practical example. Days of the month could be represented by rows, weather variables (such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall) could be represented by columns, and various cities could be represented by the third dimension. Because it can only handle two variables at once (days vs. weather variables, for example) and cannot naturally separate data across multiple locations without duplicating or cluttering the layout, a 2D matrix would not be sufficient.
  
Part F — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students

rowMeans(all_students)
```
Question #11

Explain WHY you chose cbind() or rbind() in challenge-1.
What clue in the data (shared row names vs. shared column names) told you which function was correct?

    Because both matrices have the same column names (Midterm and Final) but different student sets (S1, S2 vs. S3, S4), rbind() was utilized. Using rbind() to stack them vertically aligns them beneath the current exam columns and adds new student rows.
    
Question #12

Suppose instead of 2 classes you had 5 classes, each recorded as a separate matrix with the same 2 columns (Midterm, Final).
Describe, in plain language (no code required), how you would combine all 5 into a single matrix, and how you would check your final result is correct using dim().

    You would use rbind() to stack five different class matrices with identical columns into a single matrix. Run dim() on the final matrix to confirm that it combined correctly. The row count should equal the total number of students in all five classes, and the column count should still be two (representing Midterm and Final).

Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize the key differences between a matrix and an array, and describe a situation where cbind()/rbind() would be useful in a real dataset you might work with.

    An array expands this structure into three or more dimensions by stacking multiple matrices on top of one another, whereas a matrix is a two-dimensional grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns. When combining datasets, functions like cbind() and rbind() are crucial. For example, cbind() adds new calculated metrics as new columns, while rbind() adds new survey responses as additional rows. You can easily manipulate and analyze multi-dimensional data in R by comprehending these structures.
